transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. Lee. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Lee. Well... I suppose I'm just here because I can't seem to settle down. I feel like I'm always up and moving around. Even on a quiet day, I'm bouncing from my garden club list, to my knitting, to sorting through travel papers... and I just don't really finish any of it.
Has this restlessness and trouble finishing tasks been something you've dealt with since childhood, or is this a new change from how you normally are?

Well... no, it's not a new thing. I suppose it's always been like this. Even back in grade school... my teachers used to tell my mother that I was bright, but just... scattered. I guess I was always losing my papers, or talking out of turn... wiggling in my seat before I ever finished my schoolwork. So... yes. Since childhood.
Have you noticed a long-standing pattern of unstable or intense relationships, or a shifting sense of who you are, alongside this restlessness?
No... I wouldn't say that. My relationships are fine. I've been married for forty-five years, and... well, I know who I am. It's just the restlessness.
Would you say this restlessness and trouble finishing tasks has caused real problems for you in more than one area of your life—like at home, at work, or in social situations?

Well... yes, I suppose so. It's... it's mostly at home, and over at the community center. My husband gets frustrated. And the other volunteers... they sort of have to double-check everything I do. They can't really trust me to keep the plans straight on my own anymore. It's... it's been causing some strain, I guess.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports lifelong (since grade school) pattern of restlessness, distractibility, disorganization, losing items, difficulty completing tasks, and impulsive talking/fidgeting. Symptoms are chronic and trait-like rather than episodic, began before age 12, and currently cause impairment in multiple domains (home life and volunteer/community activities). No evidence of unstable relationships or identity disturbance to suggest borderline personality disorder, and no distinct mood episodes suggesting anxiety or mood disorder as primary cause. This pattern is consistent with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, combined presentation, persisting into adulthood.
